business_patterns.top_pattern: CA HMO acute hospital spend is highly concentrated at UCI MEDICAL CENTER
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: CA Commercial Local Group / HMO / ACUTE HOSPITAL
key_driver_codes: Degenerative Nervous System Disorders without MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: CA HMO acute hospital cost growth is dominated by UCI MEDICAL CENTER. The increase reflects both higher use and higher cost per case, which makes this a provider concentration issue rather than a broad statewide trend. A small number of very expensive neurological cases also contributed, but the main business lever is concentrated provider economics at one hospital.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: This is the largest single cost signal and it is concentrated enough to support targeted network, reimbursement, and utilization action.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Open a joint UCI MEDICAL CENTER review covering contract terms, admission and level-of-care management, and steerage options for CA HMO members.
evidence_summary: UCI MEDICAL CENTER accounts for about $5.2M of the $5.4M increase.
Claim count rose by 247 and paid per admit increased by about $19.7K in CA HMO acute hospital business.
A very small number of degenerative nervous system disorder cases added about $226K, showing high-cost episode risk on top of the provider concentration.

business_patterns.top_pattern: WI POS acute hospital costs are rising from both more use and higher cost per case
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: WI Commercial Local Group / POS / ACUTE HOSPITAL
business_patterns.pattern_details: WI POS acute hospital spend increased through a mix of higher utilization and higher paid per case. The signal is not tied to a single coded condition in the evidence provided, so the business issue is broader acute hospital pressure within this product and state. This is an operational trend that should be worked through both utilization management and reimbursement review.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Because both volume and unit cost are moving up, a single lever will not be enough to slow the trend.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Run a WI POS acute hospital action plan that pairs admission and level-of-care review with reimbursement analysis on the highest-cost facilities.
evidence_summary: WI POS acute hospital spend increased by about $1.1M.
Claim count rose by 10 and paid per admit increased by about $2.7K.
The increase is concentrated enough to warrant targeted facility-level follow-up rather than a broad product-wide policy change.

business_patterns.top_pattern: UNATTRIBUTED inpatient Med/Surg costs are being driven by rare catastrophic cases
key_driver_codes: Coronary Bypass with Cardiac Catheterization or Open Ablation with MCC
Degenerative Nervous System Disorders with MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: This is a catastrophic case pattern, not broad inpatient growth. A lung transplant and other isolated high-severity Med/Surg admissions account for most of the increase, with each event carrying very high paid amounts. These episodes need focused case review and catastrophic claim handling rather than broad utilization controls.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Rare catastrophic cases can distort trend results and require different clinical and financial actions than ordinary inpatient growth.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Route the identified episodes for transplant and high-acuity case review, confirm catastrophic claim handling, and separate these claims from routine Med/Surg trend management.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The pattern is based on a few single-case events and sits in an UNATTRIBUTED segment, so attribution and coding should be confirmed before broader conclusions are drawn.
evidence_summary: A single lung transplant case contributed about $777K.
One coronary bypass case added about $208K.
Two degenerative nervous system disorder cases added about $146K, confirming a concentrated high-severity inpatient pattern rather than broad volume growth.

business_patterns.top_pattern: CA inpatient Med/Surg growth is concentrated in rare high-cost cases, several at UCI MEDICAL CENTER
key_driver_codes: Pathological Fractures and Musculoskeletal and Connective Tissue Malignancy with MCC
Cardiac Valve and Other Major Cardiothoracic Procedures without Cardiac Catheterization with CC
Degenerative Nervous System Disorders without MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: CA inpatient Med/Surg cost growth is being driven by a handful of rare, expensive cases rather than a broad change in inpatient volume. Several of the highest-cost cases are tied to UCI MEDICAL CENTER, including oncology-related and complex cardiothoracic admissions. This calls for focused clinical review of severity, care pathways, and reimbursement on specific episodes.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Targeted review can address outlier inpatient spend without overreacting to the broader CA inpatient population.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Prioritize case-by-case clinical and reimbursement review on the highest-cost CA Med/Surg admissions, starting with UCI MEDICAL CENTER and the top malignancy and cardiothoracic cases.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The pattern is built from small numbers of high-cost cases with low baseline counts, so coding completeness and severity assignment should be confirmed during review.
evidence_summary: A single UCI MEDICAL CENTER case involving pathological fracture and malignancy added about $268K.
Another UCI MEDICAL CENTER cardiothoracic case added about $261K.
A degenerative nervous system disorder case added about $185K, with additional smaller neuro cases reinforcing a concentrated rare-case pattern.

business_patterns.top_pattern: Not-mapped facility and clinical buckets are masking true drivers across multiple segments
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: Commercial Local Group / Not Mapped facility and outpatient clinical categories
business_patterns.pattern_details: Several spend increases are landing in not-mapped facility or clinical buckets across ME, WI, CA, CO, and UNATTRIBUTED segments. That makes it hard to tell whether the underlying issue is authorization leakage, coding movement, provider classification, or true unit-cost change. This is a gating validation issue and should be resolved before broader provider or utilization actions are taken on these buckets.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: If mapping is wrong, the organization can misdirect network, reimbursement, and utilization interventions.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Complete a focused validation of not-mapped facility type, recurring DRG, and temporary code classification, then reroute the cleaned findings to reimbursement, UM, or provider teams as appropriate.
business_patterns.validation_reason: Multiple groups carry unmapped or unknown values, including facility and clinical classifications, so business action is not reliable until mapping and attribution are confirmed.
evidence_summary: Not-mapped groups contribute about $0.7M of total increase across ME, WI, CA, CO, and UNATTRIBUTED segments.
WI PPO not-mapped facility spend rose about $150K even though claims fell by 9, pointing to a classification or unit-cost issue rather than simple volume growth.
ME PPO not-mapped facility spend rose about $130K while claims fell by 213, again suggesting mapping or repricing movement.
UNATTRIBUTED outpatient not-mapped buckets added material drug, behavioral health, and surgery spend that cannot be cleanly actioned until classification is fixed.

business_patterns.top_pattern: ME PPO post-acute spend is rising in rehab and other non-acute settings
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: ME Commercial Local Group / PPO / Physical Rehab and OTHER
business_patterns.pattern_details: ME PPO cost growth is showing up in post-acute settings rather than acute hospital care. Physical rehab is the main driver, with more claims and higher paid per case, plus a smaller spike in other facility settings. This points to site-of-care and post-acute management opportunities.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Post-acute referral patterns and authorization controls can be adjusted more directly than broad inpatient reimbursement.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Review ME PPO post-acute referral pathways, authorization criteria, and intensity management for physical rehab and other non-acute placements.
evidence_summary: ME PPO physical rehab added about $151K.
Physical rehab claim count increased by 99 and paid per admit increased by about $1.1K.
A smaller ME PPO OTHER facility signal added about $69K, reinforcing the post-acute site-of-care theme.

business_patterns.top_pattern: CA maternity costs are being pushed by high-severity C-section cases rather than delivery volume
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: CA / IP OB Dlvry/Well NB / ACUTE HOSPITAL
key_driver_codes: Cesarean Section without Sterilization with MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: CA maternity cost pressure is concentrated in a very small number of high-severity C-section cases. The clinical signal shows rare high-cost obstetric admissions, and a separate PPO acute hospital signal on the same DRG points to higher cost per case rather than more deliveries. This should be treated as a maternity-specific severity and reimbursement issue.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Maternity management, severity review, and DRG reimbursement action are different from general acute hospital cost controls.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Review CA C-section with MCC cases for severity documentation, maternity case-management triggers, and PPO reimbursement terms on this DRG.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The signal comes from a very small number of high-cost C-section cases, so severity coding and case classification should be confirmed during action planning.
evidence_summary: One CA C-section without sterilization with MCC case tied to diagnosis O1404 added about $74K.
A second smaller C-section case added about $5K.
Separate CA PPO acute hospital spend on the same DRG added about $65K with no volume increase and paid per admit up about $21.6K.

business_patterns.top_pattern: CA aftercare cases are shifting into SNF and nursing facility settings
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: CA / EPO / SNF - FREE STANDING and NF
key_driver_codes: Aftercare, Musculoskeletal System and Connective Tissue with CC
business_patterns.pattern_details: CA has a small but distinct post-acute aftercare pattern moving into skilled nursing and nursing facility settings. The signal is concentrated in musculoskeletal aftercare cases and shows both more use and higher cost per case. This suggests a discharge-planning and post-acute steerage opportunity rather than a broad inpatient issue.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Post-acute placement decisions can create avoidable spend if members are not routed to the most appropriate contracted setting.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Review CA EPO discharge patterns for musculoskeletal aftercare, confirm preferred SNF and nursing facility placement, and assess reimbursement on the highest-cost post-acute stays.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The pattern is based on a small number of cases across post-acute settings, so member placement and claim classification should be confirmed as part of follow-up.
evidence_summary: CA EPO SNF - FREE STANDING spend increased by about $57K on 4 claims.
Paid per admit in that SNF setting increased by about $14.4K.
A related CA nursing facility aftercare pattern added about $57K, including three Z4789 cases and one S42321D case.

executive_summary.headline: The biggest business story is concentrated acute hospital cost pressure in CA and WI, alongside a separate cross-segment not-mapped validation issue that must be resolved before some provider and authorization actions can be trusted.
executive_summary.primary_business_message: CA HMO acute hospital spend is heavily concentrated at UCI MEDICAL CENTER, while WI POS acute hospital costs are rising through both higher use and higher paid amounts per case. Separate rare catastrophic inpatient episodes and high-severity maternity and post-acute cases require targeted clinical handling, and a broad not-mapped classification problem across ME, WI, CA, CO, and UNATTRIBUTED segments is a gating data-quality issue for downstream network, reimbursement, and UM work.
recommended_focus_order: Address CA HMO acute hospital concentration at UCI MEDICAL CENTER.
Work the WI POS acute hospital mixed volume and unit-cost trend.
Resolve the not-mapped facility and clinical classification issues before acting on those buckets.

notes: Top-8 synthesis prioritizes the most material, actionable, and validation-critical themes while leaving three low-baseline residual acute hospital groups ungrouped.
